conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly the same spot on my left side. It went away before, but now it’s back and getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. We’ll get some imaging done to check what’s going on. We’ll start with a CT scan of your abdomen and pelvis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the scan show if it’s related to my bones or muscles?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it will help us see if there’s any fracture or other issue in the ribs or spine. Given your history, we want to be thorough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The initial images didn’t show kidney stones, which is good. But we need a more detailed scan with contrast to get a full picture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that safe with my other conditions? I’m on a lot of medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your meds, and the contrast should be safe. We’ll monitor you closely during the scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your CT scan with contrast is back. There’s no sign of an abdominal emergency, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what’s causing the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The scan shows subacute fractures in your left ribs. These appear to be healing but still painful. That’s likely the source of your flank pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that makes sense. I did fall on that side a few weeks ago. But why is it flaring up now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes pain can return as you resume activity. The bones are healing, but they’re still sensitive to movement and pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need surgery or anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, these don’t require surgery. We’ll manage the pain with medication and rest. We’ll also consult pain management for longer-term support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds manageable. Anything else on the scan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There is something we need to follow up on. A new soft tissue nodule was seen in your right breast, about 17 mm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A nodule? Is that cancer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can’t say for sure yet. It could be related to an old bruise you mentioned. But we recommend a mammogram to check it further.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had some bruising there a while ago. Could that cause a nodule?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, trauma can sometimes cause benign changes. But we want to be safe and make sure it resolves. Your PCP will help coordinate the follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, I’ll make sure to follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also noticed you’ve been having leg pain when walking. You mentioned it’s been going on for a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it hurts when I walk, and it’s tender to touch. I thought it was just from the DVT I had before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be related to circulation. We recommend an ankle-brachial index test with exercise to check for peripheral vascular disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can do that after I’m discharged?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s an outpatient test. We’ll send the order to your primary care team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood work is stable. Hemoglobin is improving, and liver enzymes are only slightly elevated, which we expect with your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my prednisone? It was increased recently.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re keeping it at 40 mg for now due to your GVHD. But we’ll discuss tapering it with your specialist soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ve been worried about side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally valid. We’ll monitor your glucose and bone health closely, especially with your history of fractures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you today. Pain is better controlled, and no new issues have come up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. What about the pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home with oxycodone for breakthrough pain and a new prescription for gabapentin, which helps with chronic nerve and bone pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the prednisone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re reducing it to 30 mg daily. Please follow up with your oncologist to continue the taper safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the breast nodule?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Please schedule a mammogram within the next month. Even if it’s from old bruising, we need to make sure it’s not persistent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll call my doctor right after I get home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. You’re cleared to go home. Keep following up with your specialists, and call if the pain worsens or you have any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I feel much better knowing what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing — should I avoid physical activity?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Avoid heavy lifting or strenuous activity for a few weeks. Gentle walking is fine, but listen to your body.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Just keep up with your follow-ups and take your meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Appreciate all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll discharge your paperwork shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready when you are.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will be in shortly with your prescriptions and instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great, thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Rivera. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been having bad headaches, stomach pain, and my right calf has been hurting again. It’s been getting worse over the past few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’ve had chronic graft-versus-host disease for a few years now. Are these symptoms different from usual?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The headaches are new—constant and all over my head. My stomach pain is dull but never goes away, and I had one episode of vomiting before coming in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll check things out. Your vitals are stable, and your exam shows mild belly tenderness and some calf tenderness. We’ll run some tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need a scan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re ordering a CT of your head and abdomen to make sure there’s nothing serious going on. We’ll also check your blood work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your CT head showed a tiny spot in the left thalamus, but it’s likely not dangerous. No stroke or bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that what’s causing the headaches?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but it might just be an old change. Your neck exam shows muscle tightness and limited movement. That’s more likely the cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had neck pain for years, but this headache is different.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: True, but your MRI of the neck shows only mild arthritis, no pinched nerves. We think the headache is from muscle spasms. We’ll try a muscle relaxer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about my stomach pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT of your abdomen was clear—no blockages, infections, or new issues. You have a known gastric ulcer, so we think that’s the source.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on omeprazole. Should I keep taking it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, absolutely. We’ll keep you on omeprazole and Zantac. Your pain has improved since admission, which supports this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my leg? I’m worried it’s another clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your Lovenox level. It was low when you came in, which suggests it wasn’t fully effective. But your ultrasound didn’t show a new clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could I have missed a dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ll keep you on Lovenox for now, but your team may switch you to warfarin if they can monitor your INR reliably at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your blood results. Your liver enzymes are still a bit high, which fits with your GVHD. But your kidney function is better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood counts?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin is low, but stable. Platelets are normal. Your leukemia remains in remission, which is great news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. What about the diabetes? My last A1c was high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your A1c was 7.5%. Given your steroid use, we think it’s steroid-induced. We’re starting you on 10 units of NPH insulin at breakfast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve never taken insulin before. Is it hard?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have a nurse teach you how to inject it. It’s simple, and it helps match your prednisone peak. You’ll follow up with endocrinology soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your headaches have improved, and your belly pain is almost gone. That’s great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The muscle relaxer helps. But I still get tightness in my neck at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re adding a soft neck collar for nighttime. It may help reduce strain. Also, your rapamycin level was high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could that be why I felt so tired and achy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. High levels can cause fatigue and joint pain. We’re lowering your dose from 2 mg to 1.5 mg daily. We’ll check it again soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been skipping my eye drops because I’m scared of cataracts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But your eye GVHD needs treatment. Please resume the drops. Your ophthalmologist will monitor for cataracts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. Your symptoms have improved, and no serious causes were found.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking omeprazole and Zantac for your stomach. Use the muscle relaxer as needed. Wear the neck collar at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, start the NPH insulin at breakfast. A nurse will go over it with you. Also, keep taking Lovenox daily unless your doctor says otherwise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well. We’ll discharge you in a few hours. Your follow-up appointments are set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: With oncology and eye doctor?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and endocrinology for your diabetes. Call us if headaches or stomach pain return, or if you have swelling in your leg.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. Keep up with your meds, and we’ll keep monitoring your GVHD and rapamycin level.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to take them as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. A nurse will go over your discharge instructions and medications before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I appreciate all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You were admitted because of dizziness, headaches, and dark stools. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. I’ve had headaches and neck pain for a while, but they’re worse now. I’ve also been dizzy for about four days and noticed my stools are black and tarry for the past week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. Black stools can mean there’s bleeding in the digestive tract. We checked your blood in the ER and found your hemoglobin was low—8.3, down from 37.5 two weeks ago. That’s a big drop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh my… that sounds serious. Could it be from my stomach issues? I’ve had gastritis before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s possible. We’re concerned about a GI bleed. You’re on several medications, including prednisone and immunosuppressants, which can irritate the stomach. We’ve already done a CT scan of your head to check your headache.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And what did it show?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No bleeding or stroke. Your headache is likely musculoskeletal, related to neck muscle spasms, like in the past. But we need to find the source of the bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I also took three cyclobenzaprine tablets last night because the pain was so bad. Was that a problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s more than prescribed, but we’ll monitor you. We’ve held your blood thinner, Lovenox, temporarily because of the bleeding risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had blood clots before. Is stopping it safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. We’re watching closely. We’ll do an ultrasound to check for clots. For now, stopping Lovenox is safer while we manage the bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We did an ultrasound of your legs yesterday. No new clots were found. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. What about the bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today, you’ll have an EGD and colonoscopy. These will let us look directly at your stomach, small intestine, and colon to find the source of the bleed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they treat it if they find something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if there’s active bleeding or ulcers, they can treat it during the procedure. We’re also starting you on high-dose acid suppression with omeprazole to help protect your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. Your EGD and colonoscopy are done. The EGD showed gastritis and some erosions in the duodenum with signs of recent bleeding. The colonoscopy found diverticulosis, hemorrhoids, and an ulcer in the sigmoid colon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So which one is bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Neither showed active bleeding, so we’re not certain. We took biopsies of the sigmoid ulcer to check for infection or GVHD. We also found H. pylori in your recent EGD, which can cause ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: H. pylori? I’ve heard of that. Can it be treated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll start you on two antibiotics—amoxicillin and clarithromycin—for two weeks to clear it. That should help prevent future ulcers.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your throat culture back. It didn’t show herpes virus, so your mouth sores are likely due to GVHD or irritation, not an active infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. My liver tests are still high—could that be GVHD?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Your LFTs have been intermittently elevated since transplant. We don’t have biopsy proof yet, but we’re watching. The ultrasound showed mild fatty changes, no masses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the capsule I swallowed yesterday—where is it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s moving slowly. Yesterday’s X-ray showed it in the descending colon. We’ll repeat the X-ray today to see if it’s passed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. The capsule is still in your colon. We did another X-ray this morning—it’s in the descending colon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that normal? Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a bit slow, but not alarming. Your stomach has delayed emptying, which we’ve seen before. The capsule study didn’t show any active bleeding site, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—the capsule has passed. The final images didn’t show a clear source of bleeding, but we’ve treated the likely causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So we still don’t know where the bleed came from?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not exactly. But with H. pylori, gastritis, and duodenal erosions, we have likely contributors. We’re treating those, and your blood count is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My hemoglobin was 8.3—what is it now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s up to 10.5, and your hematocrit is 31.6. That’s a good improvement. You’re not actively bleeding, so we’re restarting Lovenox tomorrow at a lower dose—40 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Why lower? I’ve had clots before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Because of your bleeding risk. 40 mg balances clot prevention with GI safety. We’ll monitor your bruising and labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Today’s the day—we’re getting ready to discharge you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What’s the plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll go home on amoxicillin and clarithromycin for 11 more days to treat H. pylori. Keep taking omeprazole twice daily. We’ve adjusted your Lovenox to 40 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds—prednisone, sirolimus, eye drops?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all the same. Continue your cyclosporine eye drops, erythromycin ointment, and latanoprost. Sirolimus and prednisone for GVHD. We’re still waiting on your sirolimus level.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see GI in one week for your biopsy results. If they show GVHD, we may adjust treatment. Also follow up with hematology, ophthalmology, and your transplant team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I see black stools again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or go to the ER. Also watch for dizziness, weakness, or chest pain. But your counts are improving, so we’re optimistic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My mouth sores—any advice?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep using the prescribed mouth rinses. Avoid spicy or acidic foods. If they worsen, let your team know—it could be GVHD flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the headaches and back pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue oxycodone and cyclobenzaprine as needed. Use heat for muscle spasms. If headaches change or worsen, get it checked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better knowing what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll make sure your pharmacy has all the prescriptions. A nurse will go over the discharge instructions with you shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check-in before you leave. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it all. Thank you for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, one quick thing—I forgot to ask about the bruising on my arm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common with long-term steroid use and low platelets. We checked your coagulation—it’s stable. Just avoid trauma and monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. And the pending platelet studies?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Those are still pending. Your hematologist will review them and let you know if any changes are needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll follow up with them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’re all set to go home. Take it easy, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, quick question—can I take ibuprofen for my back pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, avoid NSAIDs like ibuprofen. They can irritate your stomach and increase bleeding risk. Stick to acetaminophen or your prescribed pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—should I be on a special diet with H. pylori?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No strict diet, but avoid alcohol, spicy foods, and excess caffeine. Eat small, frequent meals to help your stomach heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. I appreciate all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you’ve been having back pain. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been going on for years, but it got much worse two weeks ago when I stood up from sitting. It’s sharp and goes into my abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Does it get worse with movement? Any numbness or weakness in your legs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s worse when I bend down. But no, I don’t have any weakness. I can walk fine. I’ve also been feeling dizzy when I stand up quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s helpful. We’ll check your blood pressure and do some imaging. Given your history, we need to be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had so many issues since my transplant. I just want to know what’s causing this new pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to start with a CT scan of your chest, abdomen, and pelvis to look for fractures or other causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your CT showed your old L5 fracture is stable, but there’s new concern about T11. We’re ordering an MRI of your thoracic spine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: T11? Is that a new fracture?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It looks like a new compression fracture at T11. The MRI will confirm if it’s recent and whether there’s any nerve involvement.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Is that why the pain is so bad now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s very likely. The good news is there’s no spinal cord compression. You’re not at risk for paralysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What happens now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll consult spine surgery. You may need a brace. We’ll also adjust your pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The MRI confirmed an acute-to-subacute compression fracture at T11. No nerve damage. Spine team recommends a brace and conservative management for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. They’ll see you as an outpatient to discuss vertebroplasty if the pain doesn’t improve with meds and the brace.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. My abdomen has been sore too. Is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re looking into that. Your liver enzymes are a bit high, which could be from your GVHD or meds. We’ll do an MRCP to check your pancreas and bile ducts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your MRCP is back. You have several small cysts in your pancreas, the largest is 1.8 cm. They’re likely benign, called IPMNs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Cysts? Are they dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most are harmless, but they need monitoring. We recommend a repeat MRI in six months to make sure they’re not growing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see. And my abdominal pain—could that be from the cysts?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unlikely. The cysts aren’t pressing on anything. Your pain may be from muscle strain or your chronic GVHD. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started you on a back brace and added morphine twice daily for the fracture pain. How’s it feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better, but I’m a bit groggy. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, morphine can cause drowsiness at first. We’ll adjust the dose if needed. Keep taking your oxycodone as needed too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood counts are stable. White count is low, but that’s expected with your history. No signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been constipated. Is that from the pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Very likely. We’re adding docusate and senna to help. Drink plenty of fluids and try to move around a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve also been having trouble sleeping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can continue your lorazepam as needed. Try to keep a regular schedule and avoid screens before bed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat labs show your liver enzymes are stable. Blood sugar is a bit high, but we’re managing it with your insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know steroids make my diabetes worse. Can we lower my prednisone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. You still need it for your GVHD. We’ll work with your specialist to taper it slowly when safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. What about my blood thinner? I’ve had bleeds before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on a low dose of enoxaparin, 40 mg daily. Your hemoglobin hasn’t dropped, so it’s safe to continue for your clotting risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The spine team reviewed your case. They recommend continuing the brace and pain control. Follow up in two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make the appointment. I’m glad I’m not a candidate for surgery yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal X-ray was nonspecific—no blockage. Pain seems musculoskeletal. Keep using the lidocaine patch and flexeril.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The patch helps. My dizziness has improved too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. That’s likely positional and related to your blood pressure or meds. Keep rising slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow. You’re stable, pain is controlled, and no new issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Wear the brace as instructed, take your pain meds on schedule, and avoid heavy lifting. Follow up with spine clinic and repeat MRI in six months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my regular meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue all your usual medications—sirolimus, prednisone, insulin, and enoxaparin. We added metoclopramide for stomach discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep track. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Here’s your discharge summary and prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call if pain worsens or you have fever, weakness, or new symptoms. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick check-in before discharge. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just to confirm—the pancreatic cysts aren’t cancer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, they’re not cancerous. But we monitor them because rare types can change over time. The six-month MRI will help us track that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will review your meds and brace use. Discharge paperwork is ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ve scheduled my follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. You’re doing well. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again for all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—your bruising is from the blood thinner and low platelets. Avoid falls and report any large bruises or bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve noticed that. I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check—your oxygen levels are good, and you walked to the bathroom fine. You’re ready to go.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. Thanks to the whole team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Call with any concerns. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a great day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Safe home. Remember: brace, meds, and follow-ups. You’re doing great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve had watery diarrhea for about two weeks now. I just feel weak and unwell. I’m not eating much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fevers, nausea, or blood in the stool?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fevers or vomiting. The stool is watery but not bloody. I do have some pain on my right side, near my ribs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history of transplant and GVHD, we need to be careful about infections or other causes. We’ll run some stool tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on a lot of meds. Could one of them be causing this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We noticed you were on metoclopramide four times a day before. That can cause diarrhea. We’ve reduced it to twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t know that. That might explain it. But I’ve had this for two weeks—shouldn’t it have stopped by now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can take a few days. We’ll monitor. We also did a chest X-ray today—looks clear, no pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. My back’s been better since I got the brace last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your T11 fracture and disc herniations are being managed well with the brace and pain meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are stable. We’re waiting on stool tests to rule out infections like C. diff or parasites.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any results yet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. But your abdominal exam is soft, no severe tenderness, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I did feel a bit dizzy when I stood up yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the nurse noted orthostatic hypotension. We gave you a liter of fluids, and your blood pressure improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve had that before. Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s common in patients like you, especially with reduced intake. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your stool tests came back. No C. diff, no salmonella, no parasites. All negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unlikely. The GI team thinks it could be small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, especially with your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It means too many bacteria in the small intestine, which can cause diarrhea. They suggested an antibiotic called rifaximin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, can I take that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tried, but your insurance denied it. We’ll schedule a GI follow-up in a month to discuss other options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s frustrating. What can I do in the meantime?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay hydrated, eat small bland meals, and we’ll keep using loperamide if needed. Your diarrhea has improved, hasn’t it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s much better since I’ve been here. Maybe it was the metoclopramide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver tests are a bit elevated, but they’ve always been that way due to GVHD, so no new concern.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my sirolimus? I heard it might need adjusting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your level was high. We’ve reduced your dose from 1.5 mg to 1 mg daily to stay in the safe range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that affect my GVHD control?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t expect so. Your prednisone is still helping. We’ll check the level again as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good. What about my pancreas cysts? I remember they said to follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the MRCP showed small cysts, likely benign. You’ll need another scan in six months to monitor them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. No diarrhea today. We’re thinking about discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Will I need any more tests before I leave?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your bloodwork this morning. Hemoglobin is low, but stable. You’ve had anemia for a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I always feel a bit tired. Is there anything we can do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep monitoring. Iron studies were normal, so it’s likely related to chronic disease. No transfusion needed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood thinner? I remember I had another clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you have a small clot in your right leg. You’ll stay on enoxaparin 40 mg daily, same as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it a new clot or old?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s unclear—could be recanalizing old clot. But with your history, we’re keeping you on anticoagulation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge today. You’ve been off diarrhea, labs are stable, and pain is controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking your meds as listed. The visiting nurse will help you with injections and meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the sirolimus level?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, get it checked before your morning dose, as instructed. Also, follow up with GI in a month.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pancreas scan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Schedule the MRCP in six months. Call radiology to set it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call if diarrhea returns or you feel lightheaded. Otherwise, take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just confirming—you’re cleared to go home. The nurse will go over your meds one more time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve got the list. I’ll follow up on all the tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll see you in follow-up. Take it easy, and wear your back brace as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for taking such good care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Get some rest and stay hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Doctor, one last thing—should I avoid any foods?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stick to low-fat, easy-to-digest foods for now. Avoid heavy or greasy meals that might upset your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. No fried food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And keep using the loperamide only if diarrhea comes back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. The transport team will take you home shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. You were admitted for nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. How are you feeling right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’m feeling a bit better since the IV fluids in the ER. Still a little nauseous, but no vomiting today. My stomach burns in the middle, but it gets better after I go to the bathroom.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And the diarrhea—how many times a day? Is it watery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, watery and yellow. I had four episodes the day before I came in. Not at night, though. And I’ve barely eaten all weekend—last thing was a small chicken sandwich.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. You also mentioned feeling lightheaded when standing. Is that new or something you’ve had before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s been going on for a while. I’ve had it since my transplant. Sometimes my heart races too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, we’ll check your blood pressure sitting and standing. We’ll also monitor your heart rate. We’re going to run some tests to figure out what’s causing the nausea and slow digestion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it my stomach not emptying? I’ve felt like food just sits there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a possibility. Given your history of diabetes from steroids and your medications, we’re concerned about gastroparesis. We’ll schedule a gastric emptying study to check that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on Reglan before. It helped, but I stopped because of the diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We may restart it at a lower dose. We’ll watch closely. For now, let’s start with clear liquids and see how you tolerate them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs show your liver enzymes are elevated—ALT and AST are high. We’re concerned this could be related to your GVHD. We’d like to do a liver biopsy to check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A biopsy? Is that safe? I’ve never had one before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s safe. It’s done with ultrasound guidance, and you’ll get light sedation. The goal is to see if your liver is affected by GVHD, so we can adjust your prednisone dose safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, if it helps us figure things out, I’ll do it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The liver biopsy was done this morning. Two samples were taken, no complications. We’ll get results in a few days. How’s your stomach today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still full feeling. I tried soup last night and didn’t finish it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on IV fluids for now. The gastric emptying study is scheduled for tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The gastric emptying study is back. It shows 85% of food still in your stomach after four hours. That’s severely delayed. You have gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why I feel so full. Can we treat it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re restarting metoclopramide—Reglan—at 5 mg four times a day. Lower than before to avoid worsening diarrhea. We’re also stopping the senna and docusate—they can make diarrhea worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve been using them since I was constipated, but maybe I don’t need them now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your endoscopy was normal—no ulcers or blockages. That’s good. But we still need to understand the diarrhea. You finally had a bowel movement, so we sent a stool sample.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it be an infection? I haven’t been around sick people.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’re checking for bacteria, parasites, and C. diff. Your CMV test came back negative, so it’s not that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re still waiting on the stool culture. Your heart rate has been high—up to 130. You’re not feverish, and your EKG is normal except for sinus tachycardia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been doing that for years. I get lightheaded, and my heart races. Is it dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not immediately. Cardiology thinks it could be due to dehydration or autonomic issues. You responded well to a liter of IV fluids—your heart rate dropped to 90. We’ll keep encouraging you to drink.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Big update: your stool culture is positive for Campylobacter, a bacterial infection. It’s treatable with antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Campylobacter? How did I get that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Usually from undercooked poultry or contaminated water. We don’t always find the source. We’re starting azithromycin—two doses in the hospital, then seven more at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that stop the diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should help. We’ll also keep you on the lower-dose Reglan for gastroparesis. Your nausea should improve as your stomach starts moving food along.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver biopsy results are in. No signs of liver GVHD. That’s excellent news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that means I can reduce my prednisone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re reducing it from 17.5 mg to 15 mg daily. This lowers your risk of infections, bone loss, and other steroid side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I’ve had so many fractures already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Your diarrhea has improved, and you’re tolerating soft foods. Your heart rate is stable in the 90s.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. I even had a small piece of toast this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great progress. Neurology saw you for the lightheadedness and tachycardia. They don’t think it’s autonomic instability, but we’re checking thiamine and some antibodies just to be sure. Results are pending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Should I worry about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not at all. It’s just being thorough. The main issues—gastroparesis and infection—are under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge tomorrow. Your labs are stable, you’re eating well, and your symptoms have improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take your Reglan 5 mg four times a day—before meals and at bedtime. Finish the azithromycin for seven days. Drink plenty of fluids to avoid dehydration and keep your heart rate down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the prednisone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay on 15 mg daily. Your outpatient team will guide any further taper. Keep using your eye drops for GVHD—Mass Eye & Ear wants you on those every two hours.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been doing that. They help with the dryness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Continue your insulin as before—NPH 10 units in the morning. Your blood sugar was well-controlled here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the enoxaparin for blood clots?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue daily. You’re on lifelong anticoagulation due to your history of DVTs and PE.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your primary team in a week. GI wants to follow up on the gastroparesis. And we’ll get those pending antibody tests back—someone will call if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I think I understand. Take Reglan, finish the antibiotic, stay on prednisone and insulin, and drink fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And call if you have severe nausea, vomiting, or dizziness that doesn’t improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Your discharge summary is ready, and a nurse will go over your medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel so much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well. Remember: the azithromycin is important—finish all doses. And keep taking the Reglan even if you feel fine—it helps your stomach empty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll make sure to drink more water during the day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m just glad to be going home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad you’re feeling better. Don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep that in mind. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will be in shortly to assist with discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to help. Take it easy at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe journey.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll be in touch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I understand you’ve been having chest pain when you breathe in. Can you tell me more about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started about a week ago. It hurts more when I take a deep breath. I also feel short of breath, but I can still do my daily activities.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Given your history of blood clots, we need to make sure this isn’t another pulmonary embolism. We’ll do a CT scan of your chest right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had several clots before. I’m on lovenox every day. Could it still happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, even with anticoagulants, there’s still a risk, especially with your medical history. But we’ll check thoroughly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT scan is back. Good news—there’s no blood clot in your lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s a relief. So what’s causing the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did see a new compression fracture at L1 in your spine. That might be contributing, but it doesn’t fully explain the chest pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had several of those. But this pain is different—it’s sharp when I breathe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also noticed old rib fractures. Sometimes those can cause lingering pain, especially with deep breaths.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I’ve had so many fractures over the years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also concerned about infection or inflammation. You mentioned congestion and cough—have you had a cold recently?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, about two months ago. The cough never really went away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll get a CT of your sinuses to check for sinusitis. That could explain both the cough and the chest discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your sinus CT shows acute frontal sinusitis and chronic maxillary sinusitis. That’s likely contributing to your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s a sinus infection? I didn’t have a fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not all infections cause fever, especially with your immune system changes from GVHD and steroids. We’ll start you on levaquin for 7 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Will that help the chest pain too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should help with the cough and congestion, which may reduce the strain on your chest. We’ll also keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also been more bloated lately. My stomach feels full all the time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have a history of gastroparesis. Are you still taking metoclopramide?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, three times a day. But it doesn’t seem to be helping as much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue it and add simethicone for gas. If bloating persists, we may need to see GI after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also checked your CMV—it’s negative. That’s good, means no active viral infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had CMV before. I’m glad it’s not back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also tried a respiratory virus test, but the sample wasn’t adequate. We’ll repeat it tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The repeat respiratory virus test came back negative. No flu, RSV, or other common viruses.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a cold then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it looks like your symptoms are from the sinus infection, not a viral illness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my back and hip pain? It’s been bothering me too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did X-rays of your hips. There’s mild arthritis, but no avascular necrosis. Your back pain is likely from the fractures and degenerative changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on morphine and oxycodone. Is that still okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll keep your current pain regimen. The lidocaine patch also seems to help your mid-back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my eye drops? I’ve been using them regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, keep using the cyclosporine and autologous serum drops. Your eyes are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My blood sugar has been okay. I used to be on insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your A1C was 6.3—well controlled. Since your steroid dose is low, we’ll continue monitoring without medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also checked your scapular pain. The X-ray showed no fracture. Likely referred pain from your spine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It feels better with the oxycodone. Should I see physical therapy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll discuss that at your follow-up. For now, focus on healing from the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your chest pain has improved, and your oxygen levels are stable. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about the levaquin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll finish the 7-day course at home. Continue all your regular medications, including lovenox, prednisone, and metoclopramide.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the bloating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep using simethicone. If it doesn’t improve, follow up with GI. It could be related to your gastroparesis or SIBO.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Any restrictions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Avoid heavy lifting due to the L1 fracture. Use your pain meds as needed, and keep your follow-up appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in clinic soon. Call if you have any concerns before then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been having diarrhea for about two weeks now. Can you tell me more about that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been off and on, but the last few days it’s gotten worse. I also feel bloated and have some belly pain, mostly in the middle and lower part.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any nausea or vomiting? Fever or chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little nausea, and yes, I had chills a couple of times. No vomiting, but I feel weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to run some tests. Your labs show your kidney function is a bit off—your creatinine is elevated. That could be from dehydration due to the diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I haven’t been drinking much because my stomach feels so full.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ll give you IV fluids to help your kidneys and keep you hydrated. We’ll also check your stool to rule out infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your stool tests came back negative—no C. diff, no parasites, no bacterial infections. That’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection? What could it be then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history—especially your transplant and chronic GVHD—we’re thinking it might be small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, or SIBO. That’s when bacteria build up in the small intestine and cause bloating, diarrhea, and pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve heard of that. Is that treatable?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, absolutely. We’re going to start you on an antibiotic called rifaximin, which stays in the gut and targets the overgrowth. We’ll also add hyoscyamine to help with the cramping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds good. I’ve been so uncomfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know. We’ve also scheduled a nutrition consult. They’ll help you with a low-residue, lactose-free diet, which can help reduce symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a chest X-ray today because you mentioned some shortness of breath. It shows low lung volumes and a bit of fluid, but no pneumonia or heart failure. Likely related to your abdominal bloating making it harder to breathe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I feel like I can’t take a deep breath when my belly is so full.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. As your bloating improves, your breathing should too. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an abdominal X-ray this morning. It shows some stool buildup in your colon, but no blockage. That’s common with gastroparesis and can contribute to bloating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. Should we do something about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ultrasound of the pelvis and liver came back. No ovarian masses, no ascites. Liver looks normal. There is a small cyst in the pancreas, about 1 cm, which we’ve seen before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely a side-branch IPMN, which is a type of cyst. It’s not cancer, but it needs monitoring. GI wants to do an endoscopic ultrasound as an outpatient to check it more closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll follow up with them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function is improving—your creatinine is coming down. That’s a good sign the IV fluids are helping and you’re getting rehydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I feel a bit stronger today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your diarrhea has also slowed. That means the rifaximin and diet changes are starting to work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning a special imaging test called an MRA of the abdomen tomorrow. It’s to make sure there’s no issue with blood flow to your intestines, which can sometimes cause pain and bloating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that common in people like me?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not common, but we want to rule it out. Given your history of GVHD and abdominal issues, it’s worth checking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The MRA results are back. Good news—your mesenteric arteries are all open, no blockages. So it’s not mesenteric ischemia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Anything else show up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They did note that the pancreatic cyst has grown a bit—from 1.8 cm to 2.1 cm. It’s still likely benign, but GI will want to monitor it closely. They may refer you to a pancreas center.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see. I’ll make sure to go to that follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Also, the scan shows a new compression fracture at L1—your lower back. You had a T11 fracture before, and this one may be related to osteoporosis from long-term steroid use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that explains the back pain I’ve had. Should I get a brace?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can discuss that with your spine team. For now, we’ve kept your pain meds—morphine changed to 15 mg three times a day instead of 30 mg twice, to help with stomach side effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing much better. No diarrhea for two days, bloating is less, and your labs are normalizing. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the rifaximin and hyoscyamine for two weeks total. Stay on the low-residue, lactose-free diet. Keep taking your regular meds—especially the prednisone, omeprazole, and Lovenox.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: GI will call you to schedule the endoscopic ultrasound for the pancreatic cyst. And keep your IVIG appointments. If diarrhea comes back, or pain worsens, call us right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, sounds good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re cleared to go home. Your kidney function is normal, no more diarrhea, and your pain is controlled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel so much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad. Remember: finish the rifaximin and hyoscyamine, follow up with GI, and keep taking your regular meds. Call us if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We won’t stop them completely, but we’re holding the extra doses for now. We’ll keep your regular MS Contin and use Tylenol for breakthrough pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I had the enema last night and a few bowel movements. The bloating is less, and I haven’t felt nauseous since.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Clearing the constipation really helped. Your labs are mostly normal—your liver and pancreas look fine, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the alkaline phosphatase? I saw it was high on the list.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s mildly elevated, but since your other liver tests are normal, it’s likely not liver-related. Could be from bone turnover, especially with your history of osteoporosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good to know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You just got back from your procedures. Everything went smoothly. The endoscopy showed a few small nodules in your stomach—antrum—and we took biopsies.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nodules? Are they dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re small and not bleeding. Could be from chronic irritation, meds, or even GVHD. The biopsies will tell us more in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the colonoscopy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We found an ulcer in the ascending colon and some areas of inflammation. Also took biopsies there. You have internal hemorrhoids, but they’re not causing issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could the ulcer be from my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Some medications, especially long-term steroids or pain meds, can cause ulcers. But we also need to rule out infection or GVHD. The biopsies will help clarify.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see. So what now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You’ve been eating without nausea, and your belly is softer. We’re increasing your Reglan from 10 mg four times a day to 20 mg three times a day to help stomach emptying.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the dicyclomine I was taking for cramping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re stopping that. It can slow the gut even more, which isn’t helpful with constipation. We’re starting you on Miralax daily to keep things moving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re looking well. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Are the biopsies back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. They’ll take a few days. Your GI team will contact you with results and next steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other meds? I’m still on prednisone and fluconazole for GVHD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue all your usual meds: prednisone, fluconazole, Bactrim, acyclovir, and Restasis. We’ve updated your discharge list.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And for bowel movements?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay on Miralax daily, and keep using the other stool softeners as needed. Try to move your bowels every day. Also, stick to your gastroparesis diet—small, frequent meals, low in fat and fiber.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my back pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue baclofen and MS Contin. Use Tylenol instead of oxycodone when possible, to avoid worsening constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. A nurse will go over your discharge instructions and medications. Someone will call you about the biopsy results. Follow up with your GI doctor in one to two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll keep an eye out for that call. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad to hear that. You handled everything well. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if symptoms return.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I’ll be helping take care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, yes. I’ve been having nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea for a few days now. It’s worse than before. I can’t keep anything down, not even water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And any pain with that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my belly pain is worse—around my belly button. It’s been chronic, but now it’s sharper. I also feel weak and kind of foggy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any fevers, chills, or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever, but I’ve had chills and some shortness of breath, especially when I try to walk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I see you were just here a few days ago. Your labs show your bicarbonate is low—down to 12. That means your body is a bit acidic, which can happen with severe vomiting or infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that sounds serious. Is that from the vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be part of it. We also see your white blood cell count was high when you came in—13,000—but it’s coming down now. We’re checking for infections, including in your gut and urine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on antibiotics before for gut issues. Could this be bacterial overgrowth again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s possible, but your CT scan from the ER was normal—no blockages or inflammation. We did an MRI of your abdomen yesterday to look more closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And what did it show?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of inflammation in the small intestine. But there’s mild irritation in the sigmoid colon—could be colitis. We’re waiting on stool tests to see why.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your stool test came back. You have rotavirus—an intestinal virus. That explains the nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Rotavirus? Isn’t that something kids get?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
