conversation_lines.text: Yes, but adults can get it too, especially those with weakened immune systems. Since you’re on prednisone and have GVHD, your body has a harder time fighting it off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not from my gastroparesis or the nodules they saw last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The rotavirus is the main cause now. Your chronic issues like gastroparesis and bacterial overgrowth may make symptoms worse, but this flare is viral.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I be sick?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can take a week or more to fully recover. We’re giving IV fluids and anti-nausea meds to help you feel better while your body fights the virus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also got your urine results. You have a UTI caused by Enterococcus. Because of your immune status, we’re treating it with nitrofurantoin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on Bactrim for prevention. Why did I still get a UTI?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes bacteria become resistant or bypass the protection. Enterococcus can be tricky. Nitrofurantoin should work well based on the culture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need to take it at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll send you home with a prescription to finish the course. It’s important to complete it even if you feel better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your nausea seems better today. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. I sipped some broth without throwing up. But I’m still tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good progress. We’re going to keep advancing your diet slowly. We also gave you IVIG yesterday for your immune support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, I get that monthly. When’s my next dose due?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In about a month. Your hematologist will coordinate that. We’ve also been managing your pain and nausea with IV meds, but we’re switching to oral ones as you improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The MRI showed something else—we saw patchy bone signal in your sacrum. It’s not clear what it is. We recommend a pelvic MRI after discharge to check it out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that cancer? My dad had cancer...

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not certain. It could be many things—some benign, some not. The pelvic MRI will give us a clearer picture. Your oncologist is aware and will help arrange it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. I was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. We’ve sent a letter to your new primary care doctor too. You’re setting that up, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m switching to a new PCP in the city system. They already know I’m here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve notified them about your hospitalization and the follow-up needs, including the MRI and your UTI treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are improving. White count is down to 5.5, and your bicarbonate is back to 24—normal. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly by tomorrow. You’re tolerating food, your symptoms are controlled, and you’re walking around fine. We just need to make sure you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been meaning to ask—should I restart my Miralax and stool softeners?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. Since you still have some diarrhea from the virus, wait until your bowel movements normalize. Then you can restart them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my nausea medicine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re sending you home with ondansetron—Zofran. Take it as needed for nausea, or before meals if eating is hard.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—we ordered skull X-rays because of your headaches. The images are done, but radiology hasn’t read them yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that change anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Unlikely, since your neuro exam was normal. But we’ll send the results to your oncologist so they can review and follow up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home today. You’ve recovered well from the rotavirus infection and UTI treatment is set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What should I watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If nausea or diarrhea returns, or you develop fever, confusion, or trouble breathing, come back. Otherwise, follow up with your PCP and oncologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pelvic MRI?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your oncologist’s office will contact you to schedule it. It’s important to get it done to understand the bone finding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my IVIG?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same schedule—next dose in one month. They’ll call you to confirm.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you only if needed. Your husband can help you get ready to leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand you had a scary event today—can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… I was sitting in the waiting room for my cognitive neurology appointment. I started feeling really lightheaded, like the room was spinning. Then I think I passed out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And did you hit your head or feel any pain when you lost consciousness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, my husband said I just slumped over. He called for help, and someone started doing chest compressions. I don’t remember that part, but I woke up quickly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That must have been frightening. Your blood pressure was very low when EMS arrived—around 56 over 35. Did you eat or drink anything this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I skipped breakfast. I wasn’t hungry and wanted to get to the appointment on time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be part of it. We’re going to give you IV fluids to help stabilize your blood pressure. We also did an EKG, and it showed some changes, so cardiology came to see you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is my heart okay? I’ve been worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Cardiology reviewed your EKG and blood tests. Your troponin levels—those check for heart damage—were normal. They don’t think you had a heart attack. The EKG changes might be related to the low blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s a relief. But why did I pass out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The most likely cause is low blood volume—what we call hypovolemia. Skipping meals and fluids, especially with your medical history, can make you more prone to that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do feel dizzy sometimes, even when I’m not fasting. Is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ll monitor you closely. You’re on a heart monitor now to check for any rhythm issues. We also ordered a CT scan of your chest to rule out a blood clot in your lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve had blood clots before, so I’m glad we’re checking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT scan is back. Good news—no pulmonary embolism or aortic issues. But it did show some mild compression in your spine, at C7 and T2.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My spine? I didn’t fall or feel any pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The neurosurgeon looked at it and said these are likely old fractures, possibly from your past osteoporosis or transplant-related bone changes. Since you’re not having neck or back pain, they don’t need treatment now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had several compression fractures before—T11, L1. So this might be similar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that fits. We’ll make sure your bone health is followed up with your oncologist. For now, we’re focusing on keeping your blood pressure stable with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I had some juice and toast this morning and haven’t felt dizzy at all.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your blood pressure is now 118 over 70, and your repeat labs show improvement in your acid levels and lactate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What was wrong with my acid levels?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: When your blood pressure dropped, your body wasn’t getting enough oxygen, which caused a mild metabolic acidosis. That’s improving now with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see. And my heart monitor—any issues?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No arrhythmias. Cardiology noted a slightly prolonged QT interval on your EKG, which is something we watch with some of your medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take fluconazole for fungal prophylaxis. Could that be a problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. Fluconazole can prolong the QT interval. After talking with your transplant team, we’ve decided to stop it for now. You should follow up with them about whether to restart it later.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll call them. I just don’t want to get an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re still on acyclovir and Bactrim, which cover a lot. We’re keeping your other GVHD meds too—like prednisone and your eye drops.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning if all stays stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What should I do to avoid passing out again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep up your fluid intake, especially if you’re not eating much. Try not to skip meals. And if you feel lightheaded, sit down and elevate your legs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I check my blood pressure at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s not necessary unless you feel unwell. But do follow up with your primary doctor and your transplant team. And we’ve rescheduled your cognitive neurology appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well overnight—no dizziness, stable vitals. We’re ready to send you home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. Just to confirm—I stop fluconazole and keep everything else?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. And call your oncologist about it. Stay hydrated, and if you feel faint again, sit down and call your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better and more aware of what to watch for.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve had this band-like abdominal pain for about three weeks now. It’s burning and constant. And I’ve had diarrhea—watery, three or four times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fever, nausea, or blood in the stool?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, no blood, no vomiting. But I did just get back from a trip—my first in years. I went to a rural area, and I was on doxycycline for prevention.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. We’ll check for infections. You also mentioned back pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, lower back and rib area. It’s been getting worse. I’ve tried lidocaine patches, but they don’t help much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an X-ray, and it shows a new compression fracture at the T7 vertebra in your upper back. That could be causing the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A fracture? But I didn’t fall or injure myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That can happen with osteoporosis, especially since you’ve been on long-term steroids for your graft-versus-host disease. We’ll do more imaging to understand it better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Is it serious? Could it affect my spine?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The fracture has caused some retropulsion—meaning part of the bone is pressing slightly into the spinal canal. But there’s no sign of spinal cord damage. We’ll monitor it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about the diarrhea? Could it be from the trip?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We sent stool tests. Given your immune status, we need to rule out infections like Campylobacter, which is common after travel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your stool test came back positive for Campylobacter. It’s a bacterial infection, likely from your trip.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Is that dangerous for me?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For most people, it causes temporary diarrhea. But because you’re immunocompromised, we’ll treat it with azithromycin to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take it. My diarrhea has improved a bit, though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. The infection may be resolving, but treatment will help clear it fully and prevent complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What about the back pain? It’s still really bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re arranging an MRI to get more detail on the fracture. We want to make sure it’s not due to something else, like an infection or tumor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The MRI is back. It confirms the T7 fracture is mostly osteoporotic, but there’s an acute component with swelling and some bone fragments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s both old and new?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The front part looks chronic, but the back has new injury. There’s also a small fracture in the transverse process and possibly the spinous process.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The spine team reviewed it. No surgery needed. The alignment is stable, and no nerves are compressed. We’ll manage it with pain control and a brace.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What kind of brace?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A TLSO brace—thoracolumbosacral orthosis. It supports your upper and lower back. You’ll wear it during the day for several weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting you on OxyContin twice a day for constant pain, plus Dilaudid as needed for breakthrough pain. Also, acetaminophen and amitriptyline at night to help with nerve pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been using lidocaine patches. Can I keep those?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you can use three patches daily for 12 hours. They can help with localized pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the pain today? Any improvement?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little better. The OxyContin helps, but I still need the Dilaudid sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. Healing takes time. We’ll keep the dose as is for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m worried about the fracture being from cancer. The MRI mentioned a possible lesion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. The MRI showed a small area of concern, so we ordered a CT scan to get a clearer view of the bone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And what did it show?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT is back. It shows severe loss of height at T7 with gas in the bone—consistent with avascular necrosis, not cancer. No soft tissue mass or erosion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not cancer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s not. It’s a complication of osteoporosis and steroid use. We’ll follow up with your spine specialist, but no further treatment is needed beyond what we’re doing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s such a relief. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Your diarrhea has resolved, and you’re walking well. We think you’re ready to go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What about the blood thinner? I’ve been on Lovenox.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching to a lower dose—30 mg twice a day—because of your fracture. It reduces clot risk without increasing bleeding risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All your home medications are continued—prednisone, fluconazole, acyclovir, and the rest. We’ve updated your pain and blood thinner prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I need to follow up with my oncologist, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and also your primary care doctor, pain specialist, and spine surgeon. We’ll send all the imaging and reports.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pancreatic cyst? The CT mentioned it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s unchanged—a small cyst called an IPMN. Your doctor will follow it with an MRCP in a year.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good to know.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’ve cleared you for discharge. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. Pain is manageable, and I’m glad to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take OxyContin three times a day, Dilaudid as needed, and the other meds we discussed. Wear the brace during the day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no lifting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No heavy lifting for at least six weeks. Walk daily, but avoid twisting or bending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And if the pain gets worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor. If you develop weakness, numbness, or trouble walking, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—my husband gives me insulin at night. Should I keep doing that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue as before. Monitor your blood sugar at night. If you have any issues, your PCP can help adjust it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And keep taking calcium and vitamin D. They’re important for bone healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ve been on Reclast before—should I get another dose?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Discuss that with your doctor. It might be an option later, once the fracture heals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I feel ready to go home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. The discharge papers are ready. Your husband can bring the car around.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it easy, and we’ll see you in the clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Ms. ___? I’m Dr. ___ from the medical team. I understand you’ve been having worsening back pain and some issues with bowel and bladder control. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. My back pain is very bad, same place as before. I can’t walk well. And last week, I started leaking stool—couldn’t make it to the bathroom. Same with urine—urgency but not much comes out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any numbness or weakness in your legs? Or any fever?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. No weakness, but my legs feel heavy sometimes. And I’ve noticed more bruising on my legs—didn’t used to have that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. We’ve reviewed your MRI from the ER. It shows your known spinal fractures, especially at T7, which has worsened slightly with some retropulsion into the spinal canal. But no new fractures or cord compression.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not getting worse? But why the incontinence?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The MRI doesn’t show cord compression, so that’s reassuring. The incontinence may be related to your recent diarrhea, or possibly nerve irritation from the spinal changes. We’ll monitor closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been taking my MS Contin every 5 hours because I ran out of Dilaudid. Is that okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s not the right schedule. MS Contin is long-acting and should be taken every 12 hours. Taking it more often can cause drowsiness and dizziness. We’ll adjust your pain plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I didn’t know. I just wanted the pain to stop.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. We’ll start with a safer regimen. Also, your labs show elevated white count and mild transaminitis—likely from medications. We’ll hold fluconazole and atorvastatin for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take so many pills. It’s hard to keep track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll simplify where we can. You’re also due for IVIG—we’ll give that tomorrow. Your IgG level is low, which increases infection risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You received IVIG yesterday. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still bad, especially across my abdomen. And my legs feel numb now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re concerned about neuropathic pain. We’ll try gabapentin first, then possibly pregabalin if needed. But we’ll watch for dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been very drowsy since starting Dilaudid. We’re switching to a fentanyl patch—25 mcg/hour—for steady pain control, with Dilaudid only for breakthrough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help the burning in my belly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the patch should help. The pain is likely from nerve compression due to your spinal fractures. We’ll also keep lidocaine patches on your abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had orthostatic drops in blood pressure. We’ve stopped morphine—it was contributing. The fentanyl patch is now 50 mcg/hour. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Less dizzy. But my legs still feel heavy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your cortisol this morning—it was low at 0.5. But since you’re on long-term prednisone, we don’t think it’s adrenal insufficiency. More likely medication effects.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You mentioned worsening leg numbness. We ordered another MRI of your spine to check for progression.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it getting worse? Could I become paralyzed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The MRI shows no acute worsening. The T7 fracture is stable. No cord signal change. You’re not at risk for paralysis, but we’ll keep you in the brace and using your walker.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The MRI confirmed no new changes. Ortho and neurology agree: no surgery needed now. The brace and pain control are the best options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m relieved. But will the numbness go away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It may improve slowly. We’ve stopped gabapentin and pregabalin—you said they made your legs feel sleepy. Focus now is on safe pain control and mobility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture showed mixed flora—likely contamination. No infection. And no incontinence since admission, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it was just from the diarrhea before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Likely. Or possibly from stopping your bowel meds—Colace and Miralax. We’ll keep those on your list.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver ultrasound was normal—no blockage. Transaminitis is likely from meds. We’ll keep atorvastatin and fluconazole held.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will my liver be okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, as long as we avoid the meds causing it. We’ll monitor with your PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your IgG level after IVIG is now 594—much better. You’ll need monthly infusions going forward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I’ve been getting more infections lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re updating your pain plan. You’re on fentanyl 50 mcg/hour patch, Dilaudid PRN, and lidocaine patches. How’s the control?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Still some breakthrough pain, but not as drowsy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Physical therapy says you’re steady with your walker. That’s crucial—any fall could be serious with your fractures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be careful. I use it at home too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your bruises are likely from prednisone and Lovenox. Platelets are normal, so no bleeding risk. They should improve over time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They’re ugly, but I guess I can’t stop the meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning for discharge. You’ll go home with your brace, walker, and new pain meds. Any questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another scan for my bones?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Your PCP will schedule a DXA scan before your endocrinology appointment to check your bone density.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. Pain is controlled. We’re finalizing discharge for tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready to go home. But I’m nervous about managing everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nursing will review all meds and supplies. You have home services. And follow-up with your oncologist, spine, and PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Discharge is approved. You’re on fentanyl 50 mcg/hour patch changed every 3 days, Dilaudid for breakthrough, and continue all your home meds except acetaminophen, atorvastatin, and fluconazole—held for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue insulin sliding scale. Check sugars regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the walker and brace?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Use them always. No bending or lifting. PT will follow up at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the numbness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It may persist. Report any weakness or new incontinence immediately. Otherwise, it’s stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Pain is better. I’m packing my things.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. Remember: follow up with your doctors, keep using your brace and walker, and call if pain worsens or you have new symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check. Your discharge summary is ready. You’re cleared to go home tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I feel much safer now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re all set to go home. Here’s your discharge summary and prescriptions. Use your walker, wear your brace, and follow up with your team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for helping me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Call if you have any concerns. We’re here for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee. You’re in the ICU. You were brought in after being found unresponsive at home. You’re on a breathing machine now, but we’re going to take good care of you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your husband told us you had worsening back pain and then felt dizzy. EMS found you with low blood pressure and low oxygen. You were intubated in the field due to concern for a heart attack.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve done several tests. The CT scan shows no pulmonary embolism or aortic issue, but there are signs of pneumonia and pulmonary edema. Your heart enzymes are elevated, suggesting a heart injury.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We placed an intra-aortic balloon pump to support your heart function. Your blood pressure is still low, so we’re using medications to keep it stable. We’re also giving antibiotics for the lung infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture grew E. coli, so we’re treating you for a urinary tract infection. The antibiotics we’re using cover this bacteria well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a heart ultrasound. It shows your heart is not pumping as strongly as it should. We’re still unsure if this is due to a heart attack, myocarditis, or another cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also found a left atrial appendage thrombus on the echo. That’s a blood clot in your heart. We’ve started you on blood thinners to prevent it from causing a stroke.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver enzymes are high. This could be from the shock state—sometimes called 'shock liver.' We’re watching it closely and holding some of your usual meds that might affect the liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had an episode of fast heart rhythm last night—atrial flutter. We gave amiodarone, and it converted back to normal rhythm. We’ll keep monitoring your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve removed the balloon pump. Your heart is starting to stabilize. We’re slowly reducing the medications supporting your blood pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started you on nutrition through your feeding tube. Your body needs fuel to heal, especially after such a stressful event.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your breathing is improving. We’re going to try reducing the ventilator support today and see how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—you tolerated the breathing trial well. We’re going to extubate you now. You’ll be able to talk and breathe on your own.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Welcome back. How are you feeling? You were off the ventilator yesterday. Your mental status is returning to normal, which is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel weak… and confused. What happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a serious episode involving your heart and lungs. You were in cardiogenic shock and had respiratory failure. But you’re on the mend now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My back still hurts… and I feel nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know about your back pain. The old compression fractures are still there. We’ll manage your pain carefully. The nausea might be from the medications or your stomach adjusting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a brain MRI. It shows no stroke or brain injury. Your confusion was likely due to the shock and sedation, not brain damage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver enzymes are coming down. We think the elevation was mostly due to the shock. We’ll restart some of your home meds soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did an ultrasound of your abdomen. Your liver looks okay. There’s a small cyst in your pancreas, but it’s stable and not causing any issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the infection gone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your urine infection is clearing with antibiotics. You’ve completed a full course, and your white blood cell count is normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heart function is improving. The last echo showed your ejection fraction is around 50-55%. That’s a good recovery from where you started.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need blood thinners long-term?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, because of the clot in your heart and your history of pulmonary embolism. You’ll stay on enoxaparin for now. We’ll decide later if you can switch to an oral medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re making progress. Today, we’re going to get you out of bed and into a chair with help. It’s an important step toward recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That was tiring… but good to be upright.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s normal to feel tired. Your body has been through a lot. We’ll build up your strength slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CT scan of your chest. The pneumonia has almost completely cleared. Your lungs are healing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re going to have a CT of your abdomen today because of your abdominal pain. We want to make sure there’s nothing new going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT shows your pancreatic cyst is stable. No splenic infarcts. The pain might be related to old rib fractures or muscle strain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function has returned to baseline. That’s great. It was affected during the shock but has recovered.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been having some diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked for C. diff and other infections. Everything came back negative. It might be related to antibiotics or your underlying GI issues. We’ll manage it symptomatically.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood counts are stable. You received IVIG for your immune deficiency. That should help prevent future infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re not ready to go home yet. You need rehab to regain strength. We’re arranging transfer to a sub-acute facility for physical therapy and monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your heart rhythm has stayed normal. We’ve restarted your home medications, including those for restless legs and anxiety.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m still dizzy when I sit up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your blood pressure lying and sitting. No big drop. The dizziness might be from deconditioning. It should improve with rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did another CT to check your abdomen. Everything looks stable. The cyst in your pancreas hasn’t changed. No signs of infection in your muscles.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will my back pain get worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The T7 fracture has lost a bit more height, but it’s not new. We’ll continue using the TLSO brace and manage pain with your fentanyl patch and Dilaudid as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are nearly all back to normal. Liver, kidneys, blood counts—everything is improving. You’re ready for discharge to rehab.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need close cardiology follow-up for your heart function and the blood thinner. Also, see your oncologist and ophthalmologist regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve confirmed your rehab placement. They’ll help you regain strength and mobility. You’ve made incredible progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I was so scared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been through a lot, but you’re strong. Keep up the good work in rehab. We’ll be checking in with your team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re being discharged to the rehab facility. You’ve recovered from a life-threatening event.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous but ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. The rehab team knows your history. They’ll help you regain independence. Keep using your walker and brace.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue the enoxaparin twice daily. We’ll arrange follow-up labs to monitor. Call us if you have chest pain, shortness of breath, or swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my eye drops?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, keep using all your eye drops as prescribed. See your ophthalmologist soon. They’re key to managing your GVHD.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your nausea is mild. Try the Maalox or simethicone if it bothers you. It should improve as you eat more.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve already done so much. We’re proud of your progress. Rehab will help you get even stronger. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll be in touch with your rehab team. Rest well and keep building your strength.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your husband and son have all the contact info. Don’t hesitate to call if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve come a long way. Keep up the good work. We’re rooting for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m hopeful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best attitude. Take it one day at a time. You’ve already proven how resilient you are.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The transport team is here. Safe travels to rehab. We’ll check in with your progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye, and thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye. Take care and keep healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Remember to keep all your follow-up appointments, especially with cardiology and your transplant team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I want to stay healthy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the spirit. You’ve got this. We’ll be here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready for the next step.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And we’re ready to support you. Have a safe transfer. Get some rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. You’re in the ICU because you came in with fever, chills, and trouble breathing. We’re concerned you might have an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I had a bad headache and felt so cold last night. I thought it was just the flu.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show a high lactate level, which means your body isn’t getting enough oxygen—this can happen with a serious infection. We’re treating you for septic shock.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Septic shock? That sounds scary. Is it from my bladder? I’ve had UTIs before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Your urine shows signs of infection, but we’re also checking your lungs and abdomen. You’re on strong antibiotics—vancomycin and cefepime—for broad coverage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my blood pressure is low—I remember that from last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we started a medication called levophed to support your blood pressure. But it’s already improving, so we’re hopeful we can stop it soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I just want to get through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a CT scan of your abdomen. It didn’t show appendicitis or other abdominal issues, but we noticed something in your right buttock muscle—a possible infection called myositis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Myositis? I haven’t had pain there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common. It can be silent. We’ll do an ultrasound to confirm and make sure it’s not an abscess. For now, we’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. And my liver tests are high again—like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your AST and ALT are elevated. Given your history of graft-versus-host disease, this could be related. But we also think low blood pressure may have contributed. We’ll keep watching.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We placed a central line in your left neck to give antibiotics and monitor your response. It’s in a good position.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why my chest X-ray was repeated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We needed to confirm the line is safe and not causing a lung issue. All looks good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your lactate has dropped to 1.7—much better. That means your body is handling the infection better. We’re weaning off the blood pressure medication.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. So the antibiotics are working?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re switching from vancomycin and cefepime to IV ceftriaxone because your prior urine cultures grew E. coli sensitive to it. We’ll continue for seven days total.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And what about that muscle thing in my buttock?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ultrasound showed no abscess—just inflammation. So it’s myositis, not an abscess. We don’t need to drain it. We’ll treat with antibiotics and monitor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked for MRSA, and it’s negative. That’s good—we can avoid stronger antibiotics. Your white count is also improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my liver? Any change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver enzymes are starting to come down. We think the shock episode contributed. We’ve stopped amiodarone for now, just to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that drug—it’s for heart rhythm, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’ll restart it after cardiology checks your heart function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. We’re moving you out of the ICU today to the transplant floor. You’ll still get IV antibiotics, but you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. I feel stronger already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You worked with physical therapy today, but the nurse said you felt dizzy and nauseated afterward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I got really confused and sick to my stomach. I couldn’t focus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a head CT—no bleeding or stroke. Neurology thinks it’s a toxic-metabolic encephalopathy, possibly from your restless legs medication, ropinirole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’ve taken that for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes after illness or stress, medications can cause side effects. You had lip movements and restlessness—signs of tardive effects. We’re stopping ropinirole for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I see neurology?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, as an outpatient. For now, we’ll hold it and see if your symptoms improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your mental status is much better. No more confusion. That supports the idea that it was a temporary metabolic issue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel clearer. But my back pain is worse since PT.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You have a T7 compression fracture with swelling. PT may have aggravated it. We’re restarting your pain meds—fentanyl patch, Dilaudid, and baclofen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I need that brace too, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, wear the TLSO brace whenever you’re out of bed. It helps stabilize your spine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver tests are continuing to improve—AST and ALT are nearly normal. We’ll keep monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my heart? I remember the clot in my left atrium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you still have the left atrial thrombus. You’re on enoxaparin (Lovenox), and cardiology wants to switch to an oral anticoagulant like warfarin after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had trouble getting appointments. Will they help me set that up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll coordinate that. You also need a follow-up echo in a few months to check heart function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did another head CT because of your earlier confusion. It’s normal—no bleeding or new issues. Your mental status is stable now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We all are. But you’re recovering well. Your infection markers are down, and you’re off pressors. We’re planning for discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Back to rehab?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, to the same rehab facility. You’ll finish your IV antibiotics there, and they’ll remove your central line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my insulin? I’m on a sliding scale here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been stable on a low-dose sliding scale. We’ll keep that for now. You can go back to your home regimen later if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my eye drops? I ran out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve restarted your autologous serum and prednisolone drops. You have follow-up with your eye doctor soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re being discharged to rehab. You’ve completed your IV antibiotics, your labs are stable, and you’re alert and walking with help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. It’s been a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It has. Key things: keep wearing your back brace, take your meds—including Lovenox twice daily—and follow up with cardiology, neurology, and your transplant team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the IVIG for my low antibodies?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, monthly infusions. Rehab will coordinate that. Call if you have fever, confusion, or breathing trouble.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been having pain in my left leg where I cut it on a shopping cart about three weeks ago. The wound hasn’t healed, and it’s been red and sore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And I understand you’ve also been having some diarrhea and stomach cramps?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I was on doxycycline for the leg, but it made my stomach worse. I stopped it two days ago, and the diarrhea has gotten better since then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Sometimes antibiotics can upset the gut. We’ll hold off on antibiotics for now since your diarrhea is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s good. I was worried it might be something serious like C. diff.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We considered that, but since your symptoms are improving and you’re not having fevers, we don’t think it’s active now. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’ve reviewed your history. You’ve been through a lot—stem cell transplant, GVHD, blood clots, and diabetes. We’ll make sure everything is managed carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s been a long road. I’m on so many medications, I sometimes lose track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll go over them together. For now, we started you on vancomycin just in case the leg wound was infected, but we’re watching closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is the wound infected? It still hurts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s red and tender, but the blood work doesn’t show a big infection, and the wound culture came back with no growth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No bacteria at all?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. That suggests it’s not a typical infection. Sometimes wounds don’t heal because of dead tissue blocking the process.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what happens now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve consulted surgery. They’ll do a bedside debridement tomorrow to remove the dead tissue and help the wound heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll give you pain medication beforehand. It’s usually well tolerated. After that, wound care will teach the nurses how to dress it properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds okay. I just want it to heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We do too. Also, your IgG level was low, which isn’t surprising with your history of GVHD. We’re giving you IV immunoglobulin today to help boost your immunity.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. It helps with infections, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it gives your body extra antibodies. We’ll continue your usual medications for GVHD, diabetes, and blood thinners as well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on Lovenox twice a day for my clots. Please don’t stop that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We won’t. You’ll continue that exactly as prescribed. We’ve also checked an X-ray of your leg—no foreign body or bone infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried something was stuck in there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Morning, Doctor. My stomach feels much better. No diarrhea since yesterday morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’re stopping the vancomycin because the wound doesn’t appear infected. The plan is still to debride it this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no more antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Since there’s no infection, we don’t want to overuse antibiotics, especially given your history of gut issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’ve had this problem before with antibiotics causing diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll manage your pain with Dilaudid as needed. The wound care team will see you after the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, just checking in after your debridement. How’s the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s sore, but the medicine helps. They cleaned out a lot of tissue, didn’t they?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they removed non-viable tissue that was preventing healing. The wound looks much cleaner now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I hope it starts healing now. I’ve lost about 5 pounds in the last two weeks because I wasn’t eating well with the stomach issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s significant. But you said your appetite is coming back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m starting to feel hungry again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. We’ll monitor your weight, but it sounds like the diarrhea was the main cause.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are stable, and you’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue your regular medications. For the wound, keep it clean and dressed as the nurses showed you. Watch for redness, swelling, or pus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if it starts draining?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or go to urgent care. You have a follow-up with wound clinic next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the Dilaudid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re giving you 20 tablets for breakthrough pain. Take it only if needed, every 6 hours as needed. You shouldn’t need it long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my diarrhea—if it comes back?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re adding loperamide to your list—take it only if diarrhea returns. But avoid antibiotics unless absolutely necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and keep up with your follow-ups. We’ll see you in clinic if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I was in a car accident three days ago. I was a passenger, wearing a seatbelt, and I walked away at the scene. But my chest pain has been getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You came to the ED today because the pain didn’t improve. Any shortness of breath, dizziness, or numbness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I’m breathing okay. Just sharp pain when I move or cough. It’s right in the center of my chest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve reviewed your imaging. A CT scan shows a fracture in your sternum — that’s the breastbone in the center of your chest. There’s also a new fracture in your left 6th rib.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Is it serious? Could it affect my heart or lungs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The good news is, there’s no damage to your heart, lungs, or major blood vessels. No bleeding in the chest. The fracture is stable, so surgery isn’t needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank goodness. I was worried after the last hospital stay. I’ve had so many health issues since my stem cell transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I see you have chronic graft-versus-host disease and a history of blood clots. That’s why we’re keeping you on your blood thinner, enoxaparin, to prevent any new clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Right, I’ve been on that for a while. Should I be concerned about bleeding with the fracture?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring your labs closely. Your blood counts are stable, and there’s no sign of internal bleeding. The benefits of staying on the blood thinner outweigh the risks right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about the pain? It’s hard to take deep breaths.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting you on oxycodone and acetaminophen for pain, plus a lidocaine patch over the area. We’ll also give you an incentive spirometer to help you breathe deeply and avoid pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember that from last time. I’ll use it every hour when I’m awake.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We also did a head CT to be safe — no brain injury or skull fracture. And your pelvis and spine scans show no new fractures, just old compression changes you already had.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my spine has been fragile for years. I’m just glad nothing else is broken.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s the pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but maybe a little better. The patch helps, but the oxycodone makes me sleepy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re switching you to Dilaudid, which is another pain medication that might control the pain better with less drowsiness. We’ll start with a low dose and adjust as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try it. Any other tests today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked a stool test yesterday to rule out C. diff, since you’ve had GI issues before. It came back negative, so no infection. Your liver enzymes are a bit high, but that’s likely from your GVHD, not new trauma.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my liver has been acting up. My specialist is managing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did another chest X-ray today because you mentioned right-sided pain. It shows no new fractures or lung issues. The sternal fracture is still there, but healing will take time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the right side pain is probably just muscle strain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most likely. Trauma can cause widespread soreness. We’ll keep managing your pain and encourage you to keep moving gently to avoid stiffness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs this morning look stable. Hemoglobin is a bit lower, but not dropping. Pain seems better with the Dilaudid?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, much better. I’m able to sit up and walk to the bathroom without too much trouble.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. You’re also breathing well and using the spirometer. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow if everything stays on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. What will I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue the enoxaparin for blood thinning. For pain, you’ll have acetaminophen, ibuprofen for mild pain, and Dilaudid as needed for moderate pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ibuprofen is okay? I thought it might affect my stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on omeprazole, which protects your stomach, so short-term ibuprofen should be safe. But take it with food and stop if you feel any discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the lidocaine patch?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, use one patch daily over the painful area. Also, keep using the incentive spirometer 4 times an hour while awake to prevent pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Should I avoid driving or lifting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No heavy lifting for at least 6 weeks. Driving is okay once you’re off narcotics. Since you’re on Dilaudid now, wait until your pain is controlled with milder meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. Any follow-up appointments?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your primary doctor will see you in a week. If you have increasing pain, trouble breathing, or a fever, go to the ER right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well — pain controlled, eating, walking. We’re ready to discharge you home with services for a few days to help with daily tasks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: take pain meds on schedule, use the spirometer, and don’t push yourself. Healing takes time, especially with your medical history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll take it slow. Thanks for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. A nurse will go over your discharge instructions one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in before you go. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it all. Use the spirometer, watch for breathing problems, and call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. You’ve done a great job following the plan. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You're welcome. Get some rest and keep healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I understand you've been feeling very unwell. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… I’ve had diarrhea, vomiting, and belly pain for about three days. My husband said I had a fever too, up to 101. And I’ve been so dizzy and confused.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you mentioned a cough with green mucus before this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, last week. The ER thought it was pneumonia and gave me doxycycline, but the diarrhea didn’t go away. It’s yellow and constant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Given your history—especially your stem cell transplant and being on prednisone—we need to be careful. We’ve started some tests, including a CT scan of your abdomen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been so weak. And my blood pressure dropped suddenly. They said I needed pressors?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, briefly. You were quite hypotensive, more than we’d expect from just dehydration. We’re looking into whether your adrenal glands might not be responding well, especially since you’re on chronic steroids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… like adrenal insufficiency? I remember my endocrinologist warning me about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We increased your prednisone temporarily and will monitor. But first, let’s talk about what we found on the CT scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The scan shows inflammation in your sigmoid colon—this is called diverticulitis. It’s not perforated, which is good, but it’s likely contributing to your pain and fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Diverticulitis? I didn’t know I had that. Is that why I’ve had left-sided pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. We’ve started antibiotics for that. But there’s more—we also got your stool culture back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It grew Salmonella. That explains the persistent diarrhea and fever. Because your immune system is weaker due to your medical history, we need to treat this seriously with antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Salmonella? From food? I haven’t eaten anything unusual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can happen even with mild exposure when the immune system is suppressed. We’ll treat it with ciprofloxacin and metronidazole for at least 14 days to make sure it clears completely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my confusion—was that from the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we call that encephalopathy. It’s common with severe infections, especially when blood pressure drops. You’re much more alert now, which is a great sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also placed a central line in your neck to give antibiotics and fluids more easily. The chest X-ray confirmed it’s in the right spot and there’s no pneumothorax.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt that tube. It’s uncomfortable, but I understand why it’s needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll remove it before you go home. Now, your labs are improving—white count is coming down, and kidney function is normalizing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A bit better. Less dizzy. The diarrhea is slowing, but I still have some belly tenderness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. The antibiotics are working. We repeated your cortisol level—it was low, confirming adrenal insufficiency related to chronic steroid use.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I should keep taking my prednisone as usual?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 5 mg daily. No need to increase it now that you’re stable. But if you get sick again—fever, vomiting—you should triple the dose for three days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll write that down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat CT scan shows the inflammation in your colon is improving. The fat stranding is gone—great response to treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. My appetite is coming back too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. We’ll keep you on IV antibiotics a bit longer, then switch to oral. You’re making steady progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s your eye? I saw a note about restarting steroid drops.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It was red and painful. My eye doctor said it’s GVHD flare. I’m back on PredForte and bacitracin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve updated your discharge meds to include those. Please follow up with Mass Eye and Ear soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are nearly normal. White count is 5.6, kidneys are great. We’re planning to switch you to oral cipro and flagyl tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly by the weekend. We want to make sure you can tolerate pills and that your symptoms stay under control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re now on oral antibiotics. How’s your stomach handling them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Fine so far. Diarrhea has stopped completely. Just mild soreness in my lower left belly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. The diverticulitis is healing. We’ll remove the central line today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. No fever, eating well, and your blood work is excellent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much stronger. Can I walk a bit more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Absolutely. Physical therapy will help you build strength. You may need a walker at home for a while due to your back pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my L5 fracture still bothers me. I use Dilaudid occasionally.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep that on your list for now. But let’s avoid constipation—so we’re holding your MiraLAX for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Discharge is looking likely tomorrow morning. We’ll finalize your antibiotic schedule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long do I take the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Cipro twice a day and flagyl three times a day for 14 days total. We’ll give you the exact end dates.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my lovenox for blood clots?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue 60 mg twice daily. Your history makes warfarin hard to manage, so lovenox is safer for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my IVIG? Next dose is due soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your next infusion is scheduled for mid-December. We’ll send a note to your infusion center.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. And my eye appointment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Please call Mass Eye and Ear this week. Let them know about the PredForte restart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m so glad. I feel like myself again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made excellent progress. Remember: finish all antibiotics, keep taking your regular meds, and triple your prednisone if you get sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
